paragraphs: “It must be a sign from heaven,” others hurried to add, and everyone accepted their opinion at once, without protest. It was pointed out that if the decay had been natural, as with any dead sinner, it would have shown later, after at least twenty-four hours. But this early corruption “was in excess of nature,” and so the finger of God was plain to see. It was meant as a sign. The conclusion seemed unanswerable.

Gentle Father Iosif, the librarian, who had been a great favorite of the dead man, tried to answer some of the evil talkers. He said that “this is not held everywhere alike.” The incorruptibility of the bodies of the just, he said, was not a dogma of the Orthodox Church, only an opinion. Even in the most Orthodox regions, at Athos for instance, the smell of corruption did not greatly trouble them. There the chief sign that the saved had been glorified was not that the body stayed incorrupt, but the color of the bones after the bodies had lain many years in the earth and decayed there. “And if the bones are yellow as wax, that is the great sign that the Lord has glorified the dead saint. If they are not yellow but black, it shows that God has not thought him worthy of such glory. That is the belief on Athos, a great place, where the Orthodox doctrine has been kept from ancient times, unbroken and in its greatest purity,” Father Iosif ended.

But the meek Father’s words had little effect and even drew a mocking reply. “That’s all pedantry and innovation, no use listening to it,” the monks decided. “We stick to the old doctrine. There are all sorts of innovations nowadays. Are we to follow them all?” others added.

“We’ve had as many holy fathers as they have. They’re there among the Turks, and they’ve forgotten everything. Their doctrine has been impure for a long time, and they don’t even have bells,” the most sneering added.

Father Iosif walked away, all the more grieved because he had offered his opinion with little confidence, as though he scarcely believed it himself. He saw with distress that something very unseemly was beginning and that there were clear signs of disobedience. Little by little, all the sensible monks were reduced to silence, like Father Iosif. So it came about that all who loved the elder and had accepted the institution of eldership with devout obedience were suddenly, terribly cast down, and glanced timidly at one another when they met. Those who were hostile to elders as a novelty held their heads high. “There was no smell of corruption from the late elder Varsonofy, but a sweet fragrance,” they recalled spitefully. “But he won that glory not because he was an elder, but because he was a holy man.”

Then came a shower of criticism, even blame, of Father Zossima. “His teaching was false. He taught that life is a great joy and not a vale of tears,” said some of the more unreasonable. “He followed the fashionable belief. He did not recognize material fire in hell,” others, still more unreasonable, added. “He was not strict about fasting. He allowed himself sweet things, ate cherry jam with his tea; ladies used to send it to him. Is a monk of strict rule supposed to drink tea?” could be heard among the envious. “He sat in pride,” the most spiteful declared vindictively. “He thought himself a saint, and he took it as his due when people knelt before him.” “He abused the sacrament of confession,” the fiercest opponents of the institution of elders added in a malicious whisper. Among these were some of the oldest monks, the strictest in devotion, genuine ascetics, who had kept silent while the elder lived but now suddenly opened their lips. And this was terrible, for their words had great influence on young monks whose convictions were not yet firm. The monk from Obdorsk listened to all this closely, heaving deep sighs and nodding his head. “Yes, clearly Father Ferapont was right in his judgment yesterday.” And at that very moment Father Ferapont himself appeared, as though on purpose to add to the confusion.

I have mentioned already that he rarely left his wooden cell by the apiary. He was seldom even seen at church, and they overlooked this because of his craziness and did not hold him to the rules that bound everyone else. But if the whole truth is to be told, they hardly had a choice. It would have been discreditable to insist on loading the common rules on so great an ascetic, who prayed day and night (he even fell asleep on his knees). If they had insisted, the monks would have said, “He is holier than all of us, and his rule is harder than ours. If he doesn’t go to church, it’s because he knows when he ought to. He has his own rule.” It was to avoid these sinful murmurs that Father Ferapont was left in peace.

As everyone knew, Father Ferapont particularly disliked Father Zossima. Now the news had reached him in his hut that “God’s judgment is not the same as man’s,” and that something had happened that was “in excess of nature.” It may well be supposed that among the first to run to him with the news was the monk from Obdorsk, who had visited him the evening before and left his cell terror-stricken.

I have mentioned above that Father Païssy, standing firm and unmoving as he read the Gospel over the coffin, could neither hear nor see what was going on outside the cell. Yet he judged most of it correctly in his heart, for he knew the men around him well. He was not shaken by it. He awaited what would come next without fear, watching with penetration and insight for the outcome of the general excitement.

Suddenly an extraordinary uproar in the passage, in open defiance of decorum, burst on his ears. The door was flung open and Father Ferapont appeared in the doorway. Behind him a crowd of monks could be seen, together with many people from the town. They did not come into the cell, however, but stood at the bottom of the steps, waiting to see what Father Ferapont would say or do. For in spite of their boldness they felt a certain awe; they sensed that he had not come for nothing. Standing in the doorway, Father Ferapont raised his arms, and under his right arm the keen, prying little eyes of the monk from Obdorsk peeped in. He alone, in his intense curiosity, could not resist running up the steps after Father Ferapont. The others, on the contrary, pressed farther back in sudden alarm when the door was flung open with a bang. Holding his hands aloft, Father Ferapont suddenly roared:

“Casting out I cast out!” and, turning in every direction, he began at once making the sign of the cross at each of the four walls and four corners of the cell in turn. Everyone with Father Ferapont understood his action immediately. They knew he always did this wherever he went, and that he would not sit down or say a word until he had driven out the evil spirits.
“Satan, get out! Satan, get out!” he repeated at each sign of the cross. “Casting out I cast out,” he roared again.

He wore his coarse gown tied with a rope. His bare chest, covered with gray hair, showed under his hempen shirt. His feet were bare. As soon as he began waving his arms, the cruel irons he wore under his gown could be heard clanking.
Father Païssy stopped reading, stepped forward and stood before him, waiting.
“What have you come for, worthy Father? Why do you offend against good order? Why do you disturb the peace of the flock?” he said at last, looking at him sternly.

“What have I come for? You ask why? What is your faith?” shouted Father Ferapont crazily. “I’ve come to drive out your visitors, the unclean devils. I’ve come to see how many have gathered here while I’ve been away. I want to sweep them out with a birch broom.”
“You cast out the evil spirit, but perhaps you are serving him yourself,” Father Païssy went on fearlessly. “And who can say of himself, ‘I am holy’? Can you, Father?”

“I am unclean, not holy. I would not sit in an armchair and would not have them bow down to me like an idol,” thundered Father Ferapont. “Nowadays folk destroy the true faith. The dead man, your saint,” he turned to the crowd, pointing at the coffin, “did not believe in devils. He gave medicine to keep off the devils. And so they’ve become as common as spiders in the corners. And now he has begun to stink himself. In that we see a great sign from God.”

The incident he referred to was this. One of the monks was haunted in his dreams, and later even when awake, by visions of evil spirits. In utter terror he confided this to Father Zossima, and the elder advised constant prayer and strict fasting. When that was no use, he advised him to take a special medicine as well, while keeping on with prayer and fasting. Many people were shocked at the time and wagged their heads over it, most of all Father Ferapont, to whom some of the censorious had hurried to report this “extraordinary” advice from the elder.

“Go away, Father!” said Father Païssy in a commanding voice. “It’s not for man to judge but for God. Perhaps we see here a ‘sign’ that neither you, nor I, nor any of us can understand. Go, Father, and do not trouble the flock!” he repeated forcefully.

“He did not keep the fasts according to the rule, and that’s why the sign has come. That is clear, and it’s a sin to hide it,” the fanatic, carried away by a zeal that outran his reason, would not be quieted. “He was seduced by sweetmeats. Ladies brought them to him in their pockets. He sipped tea, he worshiped his belly, filling it with sweet things and his mind with haughty thoughts.... And for this he is put to shame....”

“You speak lightly, Father.” Father Païssy, too, raised his voice. “I admire your fasting and your severities, but you speak lightly, like some frivolous youth, fickle and childish. Go away, Father, I command you!” Father Païssy thundered in conclusion.

“I’ll go,” said Ferapont, seeming somewhat taken aback, but just as bitter. “You learned men! You’re so clever you look down on my humbleness. I came here with little learning, and here I’ve forgotten what I did know. God Himself has kept me, in my weakness, safe from your subtlety.”
Father Païssy stood over him, waiting resolutely. Father Ferapont paused and, suddenly leaning his cheek on his hand despondently, said in a sing-song voice, looking at the coffin of the dead elder:

“Tomorrow they will sing over him ‘Our Helper and Defender’—a splendid anthem—and over me when I die all they’ll sing will be ‘What earthly joy’—a little canticle,”[6] he added with tearful regret. “You are proud and puffed up. This is a vain place!” he shouted suddenly like a madman, and with a wave of his hand he turned quickly and went quickly down the steps. The crowd waiting below wavered; some followed him at once and some lingered, for the cell was still open, and Father Païssy, following Father Ferapont onto the steps, stood watching him. But the excited old fanatic was not completely silenced. Twenty steps away, he suddenly turned toward the setting sun, raised both arms and, as though someone had cut him down, fell to the ground with a loud scream.

“My God has conquered! Christ has conquered the setting sun!” he shouted frantically, stretching his hands up to the sun. Falling face downward on the ground, he sobbed like a little child, shaken by his tears and spreading his arms out on the ground. Then they all rushed up to him. There were exclamations and sobs of sympathy ... a kind of frenzy seemed to take hold of them all.
“This is the one who is a saint! This is the one who is a holy man!” some cried aloud, losing their fear. “This is the one who should be an elder,” others added spitefully.

“He wouldn’t be an elder ... he would refuse ... he wouldn’t serve a cursed innovation ... he wouldn’t copy their foolery,” other voices chimed in at once. It is hard to say how far they might have gone, but at that moment the bell rang, calling them to service. All began crossing themselves at once. Father Ferapont, too, got up and, crossing himself, went back to his cell without looking round, still uttering wholly incoherent cries. A few followed him, but most dispersed, hurrying to service. Father Païssy let Father Iosif read in his place and went down. The frantic outcries of bigots could not shake him, but his heart was suddenly filled with melancholy for some special reason, and he felt it. He stood still and suddenly asked himself, “Why am I sad, even to dejection?” and at once realized with surprise that his sudden sadness came from a very small, particular cause. In the crowd thronging the entrance to the cell, he had noticed Alyosha, and he remembered that he had felt a pang at his heart at once on seeing him. “Can that boy mean so much to my heart now?” he asked himself in wonder.

At that moment Alyosha passed him, hurrying away, but not toward the church. Their eyes met. Alyosha quickly looked away and dropped his eyes to the ground, and from the boy’s look alone Father Païssy guessed what a great change was taking place in him at that moment.
“Have you, too, fallen into temptation?” cried Father Païssy. “Can you be with those of little faith?” he added mournfully.

Alyosha stopped and gazed vaguely at Father Païssy, but quickly turned his eyes away again and again looked at the ground. He stood sideways and did not turn his face to Father Païssy, who watched him closely.
“Where are you hurrying? The bell calls to service,” he asked again, but again Alyosha gave no answer.
“Are you leaving the hermitage? What, without asking leave, without asking a blessing?”

Alyosha suddenly gave a wry smile and cast a strange, very strange, look at the Father to whom his former guide, the former sovereign of his heart and mind, his beloved elder, had entrusted him as he lay dying. And suddenly, still without speaking, he waved his hand, as though not caring even to be respectful, and with quick steps walked toward the gates, away from the hermitage.
“You will come back again!” murmured Father Païssy, looking after him with sorrowful surprise.
